pages.content:
The UTXO Model: Bitcoin's Fundamental Accounting System

Bitcoin's accounting model fundamentally differs from traditional banking systems that maintain running account balances. Instead of tracking how much money each account contains, Bitcoin uses the Unspent Transaction Output model, commonly abbreviated as UTXO, which treats each unit of Bitcoin as a discrete, indivisible object with its own transaction history dating back to when those coins were first mined. Understanding the UTXO model is essential for comprehending how Bitcoin transactions work, how privacy can be compromised, and how investigators can trace illicit activity through blockchain analysis.

In the UTXO model, every Bitcoin transaction consumes one or more unspent outputs from previous transactions as inputs and creates new unspent outputs as outputs. Each UTXO represents a specific amount of bitcoin locked to a particular Bitcoin address through a cryptographic locking script, typically a hash of the recipient's public key. To spend a UTXO, the owner must provide a digital signature proving possession of the corresponding private key, thereby unlocking the UTXO and making it available as an input to a new transaction.

Think of UTXOs as physical cash denominations — bills and coins of various values sitting in your wallet. A Bitcoin wallet displaying a balance of 0.45 BTC might actually consist of several distinct UTXOs: perhaps 0.2 BTC, 0.15 BTC, 0.07 BTC, and 0.03 BTC. Each UTXO is separate and indivisible. When making a purchase with physical cash, if something costs twelve dollars and you only have a twenty-dollar bill, you hand over the entire twenty and receive eight dollars in change. Bitcoin transactions work identically through the UTXO model.

Consider a practical example. Bob owns a single UTXO worth 50 BTC. He wants to send 0.5 BTC to Alice. Since UTXOs are indivisible, Bob's wallet constructs a transaction that consumes the entire 50 BTC UTXO as input and creates two new outputs: one output of 0.5 BTC locked to Alice's address, and a second output of approximately 49.5 BTC returned to a new address that Bob controls, minus a small transaction fee. The original 50 BTC UTXO is now spent and cannot be used again, while the two new UTXOs — one belonging to Alice and one belonging to Bob — are unspent and available for future transactions.

When you receive bitcoin, your wallet software scans the entire blockchain to identify all UTXOs locked to addresses you control. The sum of all these UTXOs equals your total bitcoin balance. Your wallet does not store bitcoins; it stores private keys that can unlock specific UTXOs recorded on the blockchain. Losing your private keys means losing the ability to spend your UTXOs, even though they remain visible on the blockchain forever. This is why the phrase not your keys, not your coins has become a fundamental principle in Bitcoin custody.

Every Bitcoin full node maintains a database called the UTXO set, which represents the current state of all spendable bitcoins in existence. As of September 2025, the UTXO set contained approximately 169 million entries. When a node receives a new transaction, it validates the transaction by checking that all referenced input UTXOs exist in the UTXO set and have not already been spent. If a transaction attempts to spend a UTXO that was already consumed, the node rejects it as a double-spend attempt.

The UTXO model provides several critical advantages: each UTXO either exists in its expected form or it does not (a binary state impossible to manipulate without detection); parallel transaction validation is enabled; once a UTXO is spent, it cannot be unspent or modified; and the model allows users to generate new addresses for each transaction, providing a degree of privacy — though that privacy is limited and can be compromised through analysis techniques.

INVESTIGATIVE NOTE Every UTXO carries a complete lineage traceable back to the coinbase transaction where those satoshis were first minted. When tracing illicit funds, investigators can follow the UTXO chain from the suspect output backwards to identify all prior owners, mixing events, and on-ramp exchanges.

Change Addresses: Privacy by Design

The change address mechanism represents one of Bitcoin's most important privacy features, though it is frequently misunderstood and can ironically become a vector for privacy compromise when improperly implemented or analyzed. Change addresses emerged as a solution to the indivisibility of UTXOs and the need to return excess funds to transaction senders without revealing which output belongs to the sender versus the recipient.

When Satoshi Nakamoto first launched Bitcoin in 2009, the protocol did not include automatic change address generation. This omission created serious usability and privacy problems: if a user failed to manually specify a change output, the difference between input and output values would become part of the transaction fee, potentially resulting in the accidental overpayment of hundreds or thousands of dollars to miners. The shift to automatic fresh change address generation per transaction was a gradual evolution in wallet software design, not a single protocol update. BIP-39 (mnemonic seed phrases) was not introduced until 2013, and HD wallets — which enable automatic fresh address generation — came even later.

Here is how change addresses function in practice. When you initiate a Bitcoin transaction, your wallet software analyzes your available UTXOs to determine which ones to spend as inputs. Since UTXOs must be spent in their entirety, if the selected inputs exceed the required payment plus fees, the wallet creates a change output locked to a newly generated Bitcoin address — the change address — which your wallet controls through a private key derived from your seed phrase.

Consider a detailed example. Alice has three UTXOs: 0.138 BTC, 0.73 BTC, and 0.028 BTC, for a total of 0.896 BTC. She wants to send 0.6 BTC to Bob. Her wallet determines that the single 0.73 BTC UTXO is sufficient. The wallet constructs a transaction with one input (consuming the 0.73 BTC UTXO) and two outputs: one of 0.6 BTC locked to Bob's address and a change output of approximately 0.1299 BTC locked to a newly generated address in Alice's wallet, accounting for a 0.0001 BTC fee. Alice's new balance consists of the two untouched UTXOs (0.138 BTC and 0.028 BTC) plus the new change UTXO (0.1299 BTC), totaling approximately 0.2959 BTC.

From a privacy perspective, an external observer examining this transaction sees one input and two outputs but cannot definitively determine which output went to the recipient and which is Alice's change — unless they apply analytical heuristics. This ambiguity is intended to provide transaction privacy.

INVESTIGATIVE NOTE Identifying change addresses in transactions provides valuable intelligence about transaction patterns, wallet software behavior, and the flow of funds through the blockchain. Change address heuristics — such as address type matching, round-number outputs, and address reuse patterns — form a cornerstone of blockchain forensics and are explored in detail in Part 3 of this handbook.

Transaction Fees and Fee Markets

Bitcoin transaction fees serve multiple purposes: compensating miners for including transactions in blocks, and providing economic incentive for miners to continue securing the network after all bitcoins have been mined. Fees are calculated as the difference between total input values and total output values in a transaction. If inputs total 1.5 BTC and outputs total 1.498 BTC, the 0.002 BTC difference becomes the transaction fee paid to the miner who includes the transaction in a block.

The fee rate, measured in satoshis per virtual byte (sat/vB), determines transaction priority. Bitcoin's block size limit creates scarcity for block space. When transaction demand exceeds available block space, a fee market emerges where higher fee rates increase the likelihood of quick inclusion while lower fee rates may result in delayed confirmation or rejection.

Transaction size in bytes depends on the number of inputs, outputs, and the transaction type. A simple transaction with one input and two outputs using Segregated Witness typically occupies about 140 virtual bytes (vB). Complex transactions with many inputs or outputs are larger, requiring proportionally higher absolute fees at the same fee rate.

Fee estimation algorithms used by wallets analyze current mempool composition to suggest appropriate fee rates for desired confirmation times. During network congestion, recommended fees can spike dramatically — fees exceeded $60 for high-priority transactions during peak demand in 2021 and 2024. During quiet periods, fees may be just pennies. Resources like mempool.space provide real-time visualization of mempool state and recommended fee rates.

INVESTIGATIVE NOTE Fee rate data can indicate urgency. A suspect who paid significantly above the prevailing market rate may have needed rapid confirmation to avoid detection, settlement before asset freeze, or time-sensitive operational security. Documenting the fee paid and the prevailing market rate at confirmation time is standard evidence practice.

The Mempool and Confirmation Process

When a user broadcasts a transaction, it enters the mempool — a collection of unconfirmed transactions held in memory by each full node. Every node maintains its own mempool, and mempools vary slightly between nodes based on network propagation timing and local fee policies.

Miners select transactions from the mempool to include in candidate blocks. They prioritize transactions offering higher fee rates measured in satoshis per byte. During periods of high network demand when the mempool is congested, users must pay higher fees to incentivize miners to include their transactions quickly.

When a miner successfully mines a new block containing the transaction, the transaction receives its first confirmation. Network nodes validate the block, add it to the blockchain, and update their UTXO set. Each subsequent block mined adds another confirmation. Most services consider six confirmations — approximately one hour — sufficient for high-value transactions, though smaller transactions may require fewer confirmations while very large transactions might warrant more.

Replace-By-Fee (RBF) and Child-Pays-For-Parent (CPFP)

Replace-By-Fee (RBF) is a mechanism that allows users to increase fees on unconfirmed transactions stuck in the mempool by broadcasting a replacement transaction that spends the same inputs at higher fees, incentivizing miners to include the new version. RBF is an opt-in feature signaled when a transaction is created. If enabled, the sender can bump a stuck transaction by replacing it with a higher-fee version.

For investigators, RBF creates an important evidentiary consideration: the original transaction may have been replaced, and the txid of the original transaction is no longer valid on the blockchain. If you are monitoring a suspect's transaction and it appears to disappear, it may have been replaced through RBF. Blockchain explorers typically show RBF history, allowing investigators to trace the replacement chain.

Child-Pays-For-Parent (CPFP) is a technique in which a user creates a new transaction that spends an unconfirmed output from a stuck transaction, paying a high fee on the child transaction. Miners, seeking to maximize fee revenue, are incentivized to include both the parent and child transactions together, effectively using the child's high fee to subsidize the parent's inclusion. CPFP is commonly used by recipients of unconfirmed transactions — who cannot use RBF because they did not create the original transaction — to accelerate confirmation.

For investigators, CPFP reveals relationships between transactions. If a suspect creates a CPFP transaction to accelerate a stuck payment, the child transaction explicitly spends an output from the parent, creating a clear on-chain link that blockchain analysis can exploit.

INVESTIGATIVE NOTE RBF history and CPFP chains are preserved and visible on blockchain explorers. An original transaction that was replaced via RBF will show as superseded with a link to the replacement. Never rely solely on a txid that predates confirmation — verify whether it was subsequently replaced.

Transaction Finality and Confirmation Thresholds

Bitcoin's consensus mechanism provides probabilistic finality rather than absolute finality: transactions become increasingly difficult to reverse as more blocks are added, but theoretical reversal remains possible through blockchain reorganization.

When a transaction is included in a newly mined block, it receives one confirmation. Each subsequent block adds another confirmation. With one confirmation, an attacker would need to mine two blocks faster than the honest network to create a longer alternative chain excluding the transaction. With two confirmations, three consecutive blocks are required. The probability of successful reversal decreases exponentially with each additional confirmation.

Satoshi Nakamoto calculated in the original white paper that an attacker controlling less than 50% of the network hash rate has an exponentially declining probability of catching up to the honest chain as more confirmations accumulate. With six confirmations, even an attacker controlling 30% of network hash rate has less than 0.24% chance of reversal. For this reason, most cryptocurrency exchanges, merchants, and services require six confirmations — approximately one hour — before considering high-value Bitcoin transactions final.

Low-value transactions may accept one to three confirmations as sufficient given the economic impracticality of reorganization attacks that cost millions of dollars in electricity and hardware for small gains. Very high-value transactions worth millions may warrant waiting for twelve or more confirmations for additional security.

The probabilistic finality model contrasts with proof-of-stake blockchains offering deterministic finality where transactions cannot be reversed after a finality checkpoint. Bitcoin's proof-of-work approach trades absolute finality for censorship resistance, permissionlessness, and security derived from thermodynamic certainty — the energy expended mining blocks cannot be recovered or reused.

Key Concept — Finality Is Investigator Certainty
Once a transaction receives six confirmations, it is effectively irreversible. A suspect cannot undo a ransomware payment. A darknet vendor cannot reverse a withdrawal. A money launderer cannot claw back funds sent to an exchange. The permanence of confirmed transactions makes blockchain evidence superior to traditional financial records — it is tamper-proof by design.

Bitcoin Address Types: What Investigators Must Recognize

A Bitcoin address is a unique string of alphanumeric characters derived from a public key that serves as a destination for cryptocurrency transactions. As an investigator, you will encounter Bitcoin addresses in screenshots, text messages, forum posts, wallet applications, and blockchain explorers. Your ability to quickly identify the type of address provides immediate intelligence on the wallet software being used, the user's sophistication, and the most effective investigative techniques.

There are four primary Bitcoin address types you will encounter in investigations:

Legacy P2PKH Addresses (Prefix: 1)

Pay-to-Public-Key-Hash (P2PKH) was Bitcoin's original address format, introduced by Satoshi Nakamoto in 2009. These addresses begin with the digit 1, are 26–35 alphanumeric characters long, and are case-sensitive. They represent the simplest form of Bitcoin address: a hash of the recipient's public key.

Example: 1A1zP1eP5QGefi2DMPTfTL5SLmv7DivfNa (the genesis block address)

Investigative significance: Legacy addresses indicate older wallet software or users who have held Bitcoin since the early years. Many early adopters, including those who mined rewards in Bitcoin's first years, have funds stored in P2PKH addresses. Legacy transactions are larger and more expensive, so a suspect still using them may be unsophisticated or using outdated software.

Pay-to-Script-Hash (P2SH) Addresses (Prefix: 3)

P2SH addresses begin with the digit 3 and represent more complex spending conditions encoded in a script hash. Rather than locking funds to a single public key, P2SH addresses lock funds to the hash of a script defining the conditions required to spend. This enables multi-signature wallets, SegWit compatibility, and other advanced features.

Example: 3J98t1WpEZ73CNmQviecrnyiWrnqRhWNLy

Investigative significance: P2SH addresses suggest more sophisticated users or institutional setups. Multi-signature wallets are commonly implemented via P2SH. Exchanges often use P2SH for hot wallets. If you encounter a P2SH address in a criminal context, it may indicate a group operation, a business structure, or a user employing advanced security practices.

Native SegWit / Bech32 (P2WPKH) Addresses (Prefix: bc1q)

Segregated Witness (SegWit) addresses use the Bech32 format, beginning with bc1q followed exclusively by lowercase alphanumeric characters. Introduced in 2017 through BIP-141, they offer reduced transaction sizes, lower fees, and improved error detection.

Example: bc1qar0srrr7xfkvy5l643lydnw9re59gtzzwf3q5q

Investigative significance: Bech32 addresses indicate modern wallet software (2017 or later). They are the default for most contemporary wallets. The transaction size reduction means Bech32 users pay lower fees, which may affect fee-based tracing heuristics.

Taproot (P2TR) Addresses (Prefix: bc1p)

Taproot addresses, introduced in November 2021 through BIP-340, 341, and 342, begin with bc1p. They use Schnorr signatures instead of ECDSA, enable signature aggregation, and support Merklized Alternative Script Trees (MAST) that reveal only the executed transaction path.

Example: bc1p5d7rjq7g6rdk2yhzks9smlaqtedr4dekq08ge8ztwac72sfr9rusxg3297

Investigative significance: Taproot addresses indicate sophisticated users employing post-2021 technology. By October 2025, approximately 85% of new Bitcoin transactions employed Taproot addressing. Multi-signature transactions and complex scripts appear indistinguishable from simple single-signature transactions, degrading some analytical heuristics.

Bitcoin Script Basics: Locking and Unlocking

Every Bitcoin transaction contains scripts — small programs that define the conditions under which funds can be spent. Understanding Script at a basic level is essential for investigators because different script types create different evidence patterns and different seizure challenges.

Locking scripts (scriptPubKey) are attached to transaction outputs and define the conditions required to spend those funds. Unlocking scripts (scriptSig or witness) are provided in subsequent transactions to satisfy the locking conditions and prove ownership.

For a standard P2PKH transaction, the locking script requires the spender to provide two things: a public key that hashes to the address, and a digital signature generated with the corresponding private key. The unlocking script provides the signature and public key. The Bitcoin network executes the combined script, verifying that the signature is valid and the public key correctly hashes to the address. If verification succeeds, the output is considered spent.

INVESTIGATIVE NOTE The script type determines what evidence proves control. For P2PKH and P2WPKH, possession of the private key is definitive proof. For P2SH multi-signature addresses, multiple private keys are required, meaning multiple co-conspirators may need to cooperate to move funds — or to prove control in court. For Taproot scripts with hidden MAST conditions, the full spending conditions may not be visible on-chain, complicating analysis of what was required to spend.

Multi-Signature Addresses

Multi-signature (multi-sig) addresses require multiple private keys to authorize a transaction, rather than a single key. Common configurations include 2-of-3 (two signatures required from three possible keys) or 3-of-5. Multi-sig is implemented through P2SH or Taproot scripts.

Multi-signature is widely used by:

  • Exchanges to secure cold storage (requiring multiple executives to sign withdrawals)
  • Businesses for treasury management and internal controls
  • Escrow services where buyers, sellers, and arbitrators each hold a key
  • Criminal organizations requiring multiple participants to approve fund movements

For investigators, multi-sig presents both challenges and opportunities:

  • Seizure complexity: Seizing a 2-of-3 multi-sig wallet requires obtaining at least two of the three private keys or seed phrases. If co-conspirators are uncooperative, funds may be unrecoverable.
  • Attribution opportunities: The existence of multi-sig suggests multiple participants. Blockchain analysis showing which addresses co-sign transactions can reveal the structure of criminal organizations.
  • Operational patterns: Multi-sig transactions have distinctive patterns that blockchain analytics platforms can identify, enabling attribution to specific services or wallets.

Pay-to-EndPoint (PayJoin) Transactions

PayJoin, also called Pay-to-End Point, represents a privacy technique that breaks common input ownership assumptions without requiring multi-party coordination like CoinJoin. In a PayJoin transaction, when Alice sends payment to Bob, Bob contributes one of his own UTXOs as an additional input to the transaction alongside Alice's inputs. The result is a transaction that appears normal but violates the common input ownership heuristic because inputs come from both Alice and Bob.

From an investigative perspective, PayJoin creates uncertainty. A transaction with two inputs that appear to belong to the same entity (based on clustering) may actually be a PayJoin where one input belongs to the sender and one to the recipient. However, PayJoin is relatively rare and requires active participation by the recipient. Investigators should be aware of its existence but should not assume every multi-input transaction is a PayJoin.

INVESTIGATIVE NOTE PayJoin's rarity means it should be considered as an edge case in transaction analysis, not a default assumption. If clustering analysis produces anomalous results for a multi-input transaction, PayJoin is one explanation to evaluate alongside UTXO consolidation, exchange batching, and multi-sig co-signing.

Block Structure: The Building Blocks of the Blockchain

The Bitcoin blockchain serves as a public ledger that records every Bitcoin transaction since the genesis block. Unlike traditional databases maintained by central authorities, the blockchain is distributed and replicated across thousands of independent nodes worldwide, with each node maintaining a complete copy of the entire transaction history. This distributed architecture eliminates single points of failure and ensures no single entity can unilaterally alter transaction records.

The blockchain consists of blocks — files containing transaction data linked together in chronological order through cryptographic hashes. Each block builds upon previous blocks, creating an immutable chain where altering historical transactions becomes computationally infeasible as more blocks are added. The blockchain provides transparency through public accessibility, immutability through cryptographic linking, decentralization through distributed storage, and verification through independent node validation.

Each Bitcoin block contains a block header and transaction data. The block header is an 80-byte data structure containing six critical fields:

  • Version number: A 4-byte value indicating which protocol version the block follows.
  • Previous block hash: A 32-byte hash of the preceding block's header, creating the cryptographic link that chains blocks together. Any attempt to modify a previous block would change its hash, breaking the chain and alerting the network to tampering.
  • Merkle root: A 32-byte hash representing a fingerprint of all transactions included in the block, calculated through a Merkle tree that hashes transaction IDs together in pairs until a single hash remains at the root. This enables efficient verification that a transaction is included in a block without downloading the entire block.
  • Timestamp: A 4-byte Unix epoch timestamp indicating when the miner began hashing the block header. Bitcoin's protocol requires this timestamp to be strictly greater than the median timestamp of the previous eleven blocks and rejects blocks more than two hours in the future, preventing timestamp manipulation to game the difficulty adjustment algorithm.
  • Difficulty target (nBits): A compact 4-byte representation of the threshold the block hash must meet or fall below for the block to be valid. This adjusts every 2,016 blocks to maintain the network's ten-minute average block time.
  • Nonce: A 4-byte field that miners repeatedly modify while searching for a valid block hash. Miners increment the nonce, hash the block header, check if the resulting hash meets the difficulty target, and repeat billions of times per second until finding a solution.

Beyond the header, blocks contain transaction data: each transaction includes version number, input count, inputs (specifying previous transaction outputs being spent along with signatures proving ownership), output count, outputs (specifying amounts and recipient addresses or scripts), witnesses (signature data for Segregated Witness transactions), and locktime (indicating the earliest time or block height at which the transaction can be included).

INVESTIGATIVE NOTE The block header's timestamp and the Merkle root are particularly significant for investigators. The timestamp establishes when a block was mined, providing a reliable reference point for event timelines. The Merkle root can be used to prove inclusion of a specific transaction in a specific block — an important capability for courtroom evidence presentation.

Proof-of-Work: Securing the Network

Mining is the process through which new Bitcoin transactions are validated, new blocks are created, and new bitcoins are issued into circulation. More fundamentally, mining is Bitcoin's consensus mechanism — the method by which the decentralized network agrees on transaction validity and block order without requiring a trusted central authority.

The proof-of-work concept requires miners to perform computationally expensive work to propose new blocks, making it economically prohibitive to attack the network while making verification of that work trivial for other nodes. Miners compete to solve a cryptographic puzzle by finding a nonce that, when combined with the block header and hashed through the SHA-256 algorithm twice, produces a hexadecimal number less than or equal to the current difficulty target. This target requires the resulting hash to begin with a specific number of leading zeros — currently approximately 19 zeros.

Finding such a hash is purely probabilistic, like winning a lottery, with miners making trillions of attempts per second. The network's total hash rate as of November 2025 exceeds 740 exahashes per second (EH/s) — 740 quintillion hashes per second — representing incomprehensible computational power directed at securing the Bitcoin network. An individual miner's chance of finding the next block is proportional to their share of the total network hash rate, creating intense competition that has driven miners from CPU mining in Bitcoin's early days to GPU mining, then specialized ASIC hardware, and finally massive industrial mining farms consuming megawatts of electricity.

When a miner successfully finds a valid hash, they immediately broadcast their block to the network. Other nodes verify that the block hash meets the difficulty target, all included transactions are valid with proper signatures and no double-spends, and the Merkle root correctly represents the transaction data. If validated, nodes add the block to their blockchain and begin working on the next block. The successful miner receives the block reward — newly minted bitcoins plus the sum of all transaction fees from included transactions.

Difficulty Adjustment Algorithm

Bitcoin's difficulty adjustment mechanism ensures consistent block production regardless of how much mining power joins or leaves the network. The target block time is 10 minutes, chosen to allow sufficient time for new blocks to propagate across the global peer-to-peer network, reduce the percentage of orphaned blocks, and maintain predictable bitcoin issuance according to the emission schedule.

Every 2,016 blocks — approximately two weeks at 10-minute intervals — the network recalculates mining difficulty by comparing actual time taken to mine the previous 2,016 blocks against the expected time of 20,160 minutes. If blocks were found faster than 10 minutes on average, difficulty increases proportionally. If blocks were found more slowly, difficulty decreases. This adjustment is automatic and deterministic: every node independently calculates the same new difficulty target from blockchain data, achieving network consensus on difficulty without central coordination.

The difficulty adjustment creates a negative feedback loop maintaining Bitcoin's supply schedule. When Bitcoin's price rises, mining becomes more profitable, attracting additional miners and increasing total network hash rate. As hash rate increases, blocks are found faster than every 10 minutes. At the next adjustment, difficulty increases to compensate. Conversely, when price falls or large miners shut down, hash rate decreases, blocks slow, and difficulty decreases at the next adjustment. This mechanism ensures that Bitcoin's approximately 21 million supply cap remains intact regardless of mining participation, technological improvements, or fluctuations in electricity costs.

Hash Rate, Network Security, and Orphan Blocks

Hash Rate and Network Security

Hash rate represents the total computational power directed at mining Bitcoin. A higher hash rate means more energy and hardware investment in securing the network, making attacks more expensive. As of November 2025, the 740+ EH/s hash rate makes a 51% attack — where an attacker controls enough mining power to rewrite blockchain history — economically prohibitive. The hardware and electricity costs of acquiring 51% of global hash rate would run into the tens of billions of dollars.

For investigators, hash rate and mining concentration data matter because:

  • Mining pool attribution can link transactions to specific geographic regions or entities.
  • The geographic distribution of hash rate reveals jurisdictions with significant mining operations.
  • Sudden hash rate drops may indicate regulatory crackdowns, infrastructure failures, or coordinated attacks that could affect transaction confirmation times.

Orphan Blocks and Chain Reorganizations

Occasionally, two miners find valid blocks nearly simultaneously. The network temporarily splits as some nodes receive one block first and others receive the competing block. The block that ultimately becomes part of the longest chain is confirmed; the other becomes an orphan block (or stale block). Transactions in the orphan block that were not included in the winning block return to the mempool.

A chain reorganization (reorg) occurs when a competing chain becomes longer than the previously accepted chain, causing nodes to switch to the new chain. Small reorgs of one or two blocks occur naturally and are harmless. Large reorgs are extremely rare and would indicate a major attack or network partition.

For investigators, reorgs matter because:

  • A transaction that appeared confirmed may become unconfirmed if its block becomes orphaned.
  • Deep reorgs could theoretically enable double-spending attacks, though Bitcoin's hash rate makes this practically impossible.
  • Orphan blocks are still visible on blockchain explorers and may contain evidence of attempted attacks or network anomalies.

Timestamp Analysis for Investigators

Bitcoin block timestamps provide valuable investigative information, though they require careful interpretation:

  • Transaction confirmation times establish when a transaction was permanently recorded. This can prove or disprove alibis, establish timelines, and correlate blockchain activity with other evidence.
  • Block interval analysis can reveal unusual patterns. If blocks are found unusually quickly or slowly, it may indicate hash rate changes or mining pool behavior.
  • Timestamp manipulation is theoretically possible within the protocol's two-hour window, but miners have no incentive to falsify timestamps significantly. Timestamps are generally reliable within hours.
  • Time zone inference from transaction patterns — not block timestamps directly, but the times when specific addresses tend to transact — can suggest geographic locations of suspects.
INVESTIGATIVE NOTE When documenting blockchain evidence, always record both the block height and the block timestamp for each relevant transaction. Block height is immutable and unambiguous; block timestamp is reliable within hours. Together they establish a verifiable, tamper-proof timeline that can be independently confirmed by any party running a full node.

Private Keys, Public Keys, and Address Derivation

At the heart of every Bitcoin wallet lies a pair of cryptographic keys: a private key and a public key. The private key is a randomly generated 256-bit number — a number so large that guessing it is mathematically impossible with current technology. The public key is derived from the private key through elliptic curve multiplication, a one-way mathematical function. The Bitcoin address is then derived from the public key through additional hashing operations.

The private key is the ultimate proof of ownership in Bitcoin. Anyone who possesses the private key corresponding to an address can spend the bitcoins locked to that address. There is no password reset, no customer service, and no authority that can recover a lost private key. If a private key is lost, the bitcoins it controls are permanently unspendable. If a private key is stolen, the thief has complete and irreversible control over the funds.

For investigators, private keys are the most critical piece of evidence. A seized private key definitively proves control over an address. A private key found on a suspect's device is more conclusive than almost any other form of evidence because it demonstrates the technical capacity to spend funds from that address.

Public keys are revealed when a Bitcoin address is spent from — the unlocking script includes the public key. For addresses that have never been spent from, the public key is not visible on the blockchain; only the hash of the public key (the address) is visible. This provides a minor security benefit: if quantum computing ever threatens elliptic curve cryptography, addresses that have never been spent from remain slightly more secure because the public key has not been revealed.

INVESTIGATIVE NOTE Private keys are the holy grail of a Bitcoin investigation. A private key found on a suspect's device, in a text file, or in a password manager definitively proves control over the corresponding address. Treat any recovered private key as direct evidence of asset control, with the same evidentiary weight as seized physical currency.

Wallet Import Format (WIF)

The Wallet Import Format (WIF) is a standardized way of encoding private keys for easy import into wallet software. WIF encodes the 256-bit private key along with a version byte and checksum, then applies Base58Check encoding to produce a human-readable string.

A WIF private key typically starts with K or L (for compressed public keys) or 5 (for uncompressed public keys) and is 51 or 52 characters long.

Example WIF (compressed): L1aW4aubDFB7yfras2S1mN3bqg9nwySY8nkoLmJebSLD5BWv3ENZ

For investigators, recognizing WIF strings in seized data is critical. A WIF found in a text file, email, or chat message may be the only evidence needed to prove control over significant Bitcoin holdings. WIF strings should be treated with the same sensitivity as seized currency — they are direct evidence of asset control.

INVESTIGATIVE NOTE When reviewing seized digital media, search for strings beginning with K, L, or 5 that are 51–52 characters long — these are candidate WIF-encoded private keys. Forensic keyword lists should include WIF prefix patterns. A single WIF string in a text file or chat log can unlock the entire balance of a Bitcoin address.

Hierarchical Deterministic (HD) Wallets: BIP-32, BIP-39, BIP-44, BIP-84

Modern Bitcoin wallets use a system called Hierarchical Deterministic (HD) wallets, defined in a series of Bitcoin Improvement Proposals. HD wallets derive essentially unlimited numbers of addresses from a single seed using deterministic mathematical functions. If you have the seed, you can regenerate every address, every private key, and every transaction ever associated with that wallet.

BIPNamePurposeInvestigative Relevance
BIP-32Hierarchical Deterministic WalletsDefines derivation of a tree of keys from a single master key; virtually unlimited child keys, each with its own private key and addressSeizing the master key recovers all child addresses and keys
BIP-39Mnemonic Code for Generating Deterministic KeysEncodes the wallet seed as 12, 18, or 24 human-readable words from a standardized 2,048-word list, plus a checksumA seized seed phrase reconstructs the entire wallet
BIP-44Multi-Account Hierarchy for Deterministic WalletsStandardized derivation path: m / purpose' / cointype' / account' / change / addressindexDerivation paths reveal wallet software type and address generation order
BIP-84Derivation scheme for P2WPKH based accountsDefines Native SegWit derivation path m/84'/0'/0'/0/0Path fingerprinting identifies wallet software (e.g., Wasabi, Sparrow)

Common Bitcoin derivation paths:

  • Legacy (P2PKH): m/44'/0'/0'/0/0
  • SegWit P2SH-wrapped: m/49'/0'/0'/0/0
  • Native SegWit (P2WPKH): m/84'/0'/0'/0/0
  • Taproot (P2TR): m/86'/0'/0'/0/0

The change component (0 or 1) in the path distinguishes receiving addresses (0) from change addresses (1). Modern wallets automatically generate new change addresses for every transaction by incrementing the address index along the change branch.

For investigators, understanding BIP-32/39/44/84 is essential because:

  • A seized seed phrase reveals the entire wallet — every address, every transaction, every balance.
  • A seized xpub (extended public key) reveals every receiving address in a wallet (but not private keys), enabling investigators to monitor all incoming transactions without being able to spend.
  • Derivation paths can reveal what type of wallet software was used and when addresses were generated.
  • Wallet fingerprinting through derivation path analysis can link addresses to specific wallet software, providing attribution intelligence.

Seed Phrases and Mnemonic Recovery

Seed phrases are a critical piece of evidence in a Bitcoin investigation. A 12- or 24-word seed phrase is effectively the master key to a Bitcoin wallet. If you recover a suspect's seed phrase, you can:

  • Generate every address the wallet has ever used
  • View every transaction and current balance
  • Move funds (if authorized by court order)
  • Provide definitive proof of address control in court

Where seed phrases hide in evidence:

  • Written on paper, metal plates, or other physical backup media
  • Stored in password managers, note applications, or cloud storage
  • Photographed or screenshotted on seized devices
  • Communicated through encrypted messaging apps
  • Embedded in steganographic images or files
  • Memorized by the suspect (brain wallet — rare and risky)

Investigative technique for seed phrases: When examining seized devices, search for text files containing 12 or 24 English words from the BIP-39 wordlist, screenshots of wallet setup screens, QR codes (many wallets display seed phrases as scannable QR codes), metal plates or specialized backup devices, password manager entries labeled Bitcoin, crypto, or recovery, and photos of handwritten word lists.

Warning — Seed Phrase Handling Is Evidence Handling
A seed phrase is a cryptographic key that controls real value. If you photograph, transcribe, or store a seed phrase, you become a potential target for compromise. Seed phrases must be handled with strict chain of custody, encrypted storage, and access logging. Never store seed phrases in unencrypted form. Never transmit seed phrases over unencrypted channels. Never leave seed phrase evidence unsecured. A leaked seed phrase can result in stolen assets, compromised investigations, and professional misconduct allegations.

Hot Wallets vs. Cold Wallets

Cold Wallets — Higher Security

Cold wallets maintain private keys offline. They include hardware wallets, paper wallets, and air-gapped computers. Cold wallets are significantly more secure against remote attacks but less convenient for frequent transactions.

  • Hardware wallets (Ledger, Trezor, KeepKey, Coldcard) store private keys in secure hardware elements, never exposing them to internet-connected computers
  • Paper wallets store keys printed on paper — secure from remote attack but fragile
  • Air-gapped computers sign transactions offline
  • For investigators: Cold wallets require physical seizure. A hardware wallet is useless without the PIN and the device itself. Finding the seed phrase backup is often more productive than attempting to break the device PIN.

Hot Wallets — Higher Exposure

Hot wallets are connected to the internet. They include mobile wallet apps, desktop software wallets, and exchange web wallets. Convenient but vulnerable to hacking, malware, and remote compromise.

  • Mobile wallet apps (BlueWallet, Trust Wallet, Exodus) store keys on the device
  • Desktop wallets (Bitcoin Core, Electrum, Wasabi) store keys on the computer
  • Exchange web wallets — the exchange holds custody; user has an account claim
  • For investigators: Hot wallets on seized devices may contain private keys in memory, cached wallet data, or accessible applications. Mobile forensic tools can often extract hot wallet data from unlocked devices. Exchange wallets require legal process to the exchange rather than device seizure.

Hardware Wallets and the wallet.dat File

Hardware Wallets

Hardware wallets (Ledger, Trezor, KeepKey, Coldcard) are dedicated devices that store private keys in secure hardware elements, never exposing them to internet-connected computers. They are the gold standard for Bitcoin security and are increasingly common among serious Bitcoin users, including criminals storing significant proceeds.

Hardware wallets generate seed phrases during setup, require PIN entry for access, and sign transactions internally before broadcasting the signed transaction to a connected computer. The private keys never leave the secure element.

For investigators:

  • Seizing a hardware wallet without the PIN or seed phrase is often futile. After a limited number of incorrect PIN attempts (typically 3–16, depending on the device), the wallet wipes itself or implements escalating time delays.
  • The seed phrase backup is the ultimate target. Most hardware wallet users write down their seed phrase. Finding the seed phrase backup is often more productive than attempting to break the device PIN.
  • Wallet fingerprints may be visible on the device: firmware version, installed apps, and device model can suggest when the wallet was acquired.
  • Companion apps on connected computers or phones may contain metadata, address caches, or transaction histories even if they do not contain private keys.

The wallet.dat File

Bitcoin Core, the reference implementation of Bitcoin, stores wallet data in a file called wallet.dat. This Berkeley DB database file contains:

  • Private keys for all addresses in the wallet
  • Metadata about transactions
  • Address labels and comments
  • Keypool (pre-generated keys for future addresses)

For investigators, wallet.dat files are direct evidence of Bitcoin control. They can be extracted from seized computers running Bitcoin Core and examined using forensic tools or Bitcoin Core itself in a sandboxed environment. The wallet.dat may be password-encrypted, in which case forensic password cracking tools (Hashcat, John the Ripper) may be necessary.

INVESTIGATIVE NOTE When you seize a device that may contain Bitcoin wallet data, follow this priority sequence: (1) Preserve device state — do not power off an unlocked device; enable airplane mode and document the screen state. (2) Photograph visible wallets — if a wallet app is open, photograph balances, addresses, QR codes, and transaction histories before touching the device. (3) Forensic imaging — have digital forensics create a full image before any examination. (4) Search for seed phrases using BIP-39 keyword lists. (5) Identify wallet applications: Bitcoin Core, Electrum, Samourai, Wasabi, BlueWallet, Exodus, Trust Wallet, Ledger Live, Trezor Suite. (6) Extract wallet files: wallet.dat for Bitcoin Core; JSON files for Electrum; encrypted app databases for mobile wallets. (7) Check cloud backups via subpoena. (8) Examine browser data for web wallet cookies and cached pages.

Multi-Signature Wallets: Key Management Perspective

Multi-signature wallets were addressed in Lesson 2.2 from an address perspective, but they deserve emphasis from a key management standpoint. In a multi-sig setup, multiple parties hold separate seed phrases or private keys, and a predefined number of signatures are required to spend funds.

For investigators, multi-sig key management creates unique challenges:

  • Partial key recovery is insufficient. A 2-of-3 multi-sig requires two keys. Recovering one key from one suspect does not enable spending or full proof of control.
  • Key distribution reveals organization structure. If three co-conspirators each hold one key, the multi-sig structure reveals the minimum number of participants and their coordination requirements.
  • Coordinator services may maintain records. Some multi-sig setups use coordinator services (Casa, Unchained Capital) that help manage the multi-sig process. These services may have customer records.
  • Hardware wallet combinations are common in multi-sig. Each co-signer may use a separate hardware wallet, meaning seizure of one device yields only one key.

Investigator Checklist — Wallet and Key Evidence
☐ I have identified all wallet applications on seized devices
☐ I have searched for seed phrases using BIP-39 keyword lists
☐ I have extracted wallet files (wallet.dat, Electrum files, mobile app databases)
☐ I have documented whether wallets are hot, cold, hardware, or exchange-based
☐ I have assessed whether multi-sig setups require additional keys for seizure
☐ I have secured all recovered seed phrases with encryption and chain of custody
☐ I have consulted forensic specialists for password-protected wallet files
☐ I have subpoenaed cloud backup providers for wallet-related data
☐ I have checked for hardware wallet companion applications and seed phrase backups
☐ I have generated all addresses from recovered seed phrases to map the full wallet

Pseudonymity vs. Anonymity: Understanding the Privacy Landscape

Pseudonymity — What Bitcoin Provides

Your identity is represented by cryptographic addresses rather than your legal name. Every transaction is recorded on the blockchain and associated with your Bitcoin addresses, but those addresses are not inherently linked to your real-world identity — analogous to writing under a pen name. The pseudonym protects your privacy only so long as nobody discovers the link between your pen name and your real identity.

  • Transaction history is public and permanently visible
  • Addresses are not natively linked to identity
  • Identity linkage occurs through KYC at exchanges, IP monitoring, behavioral patterns, and OSINT
  • Privacy erodes over time as more data points accumulate

Anonymity — What Bitcoin Does Not Provide

True anonymity means your transactions are not linkable to you even in principle, or that linking them requires breaking strong cryptographic assumptions. Privacy-focused cryptocurrencies like Monero and Zcash implement cryptographic anonymity through ring signatures, confidential transactions, and zero-knowledge proofs that mathematically obscure transaction participants and amounts.

  • Bitcoin does not implement ring signatures or confidential transactions
  • Every transaction amount is permanently visible on-chain
  • All addresses are visible to any blockchain observer
  • Strong anonymity requires additional layers that Bitcoin does not natively provide

Bitcoin's pseudonymity operates within a completely transparent system. Every transaction ever conducted is permanently recorded on the blockchain and publicly visible to anyone who runs a full node or uses a blockchain explorer. Observers can see which addresses sent funds, which addresses received funds, and the exact amounts transferred. They can trace the entire history of any UTXO back to the coinbase transaction where those satoshis were first mined.

The critical vulnerability is that Bitcoin addresses, while pseudonymous, can be linked to real-world identities through numerous vectors:

  • KYC at exchanges: Centralized exchanges must collect identification documents, proof of address, facial photos, and other personal information. Law enforcement can subpoena these records; data breaches can expose them publicly.
  • IP address monitoring: When you broadcast a Bitcoin transaction, your IP address can be associated with that transaction by network observers. Most users do not use Tor or VPNs.
  • Behavioral deanonymization: Publicly posting a Bitcoin address on social media, reusing addresses across services, or discussing transactions in forums creates links between pseudonymous addresses and online identity.
  • Transaction graph analysis: Consolidating UTXOs from multiple sources or sending change to predictable address types leaks ownership information over time.

The permanence of blockchain records exacerbates privacy risks. Even if you maintain perfect privacy today, a single future mistake — such as sending funds from an old address to a KYC exchange — can retroactively deanonymize your entire transaction history.

INVESTIGATIVE NOTE Bitcoin's pseudonymity model creates tiered privacy exposure. At the lowest tier, users who conduct all transactions through KYC exchanges have essentially zero privacy from regulators and law enforcement. At a middle tier, users who withdraw to personal wallets and avoid address reuse gain privacy from casual observers but remain vulnerable to professional blockchain analysis. The highest native tier — CoinJoin, full nodes, Tor, rigorous operational security — still remains exposed to well-resourced state actors.

Change Addresses, Address Reuse, and Their Investigative Consequences

Change Addresses and Their Role in Privacy

The change address mechanism (covered technically in Lesson 2.1) serves critical privacy purposes. By returning change to a freshly generated address with no prior transaction history, Bitcoin's design attempts to obscure which output is the payment and which is change, making transaction analysis more difficult.

However, users who do not understand how change addresses work may be confused when checking a block explorer, seeing larger amounts being transferred than they intended to send. This is not theft or error — it represents the full UTXO being spent with change returned to a newly created address under their control.

From an investigative perspective, identifying change addresses in transactions provides valuable intelligence about transaction patterns, wallet software behavior, and the flow of funds through the blockchain. Change address heuristics form a cornerstone of blockchain forensics.

Address Reuse and Its Consequences

The foundational privacy practice is avoiding address reuse. Bitcoin's design intends users to generate and use a new address for every transaction, both for receiving payments and for change outputs. Address reuse creates an obvious link between transactions, making clustering of a user's addresses straightforward. Modern HD wallets automatically generate new addresses, but users must ensure their wallet software follows best practices and avoid manually reusing addresses for convenience.

For investigators, address reuse is a significant opportunity. A suspect who reuses addresses creates a single point of aggregation that links all their transactions together. Exchange deposit addresses that are reused create permanent bridges between the exchange account and all activity on that address. Social media posts containing donation addresses that are reused create direct links between online identities and transaction histories.

INVESTIGATIVE NOTE When analyzing a suspect's blockchain activity, begin by searching for address reuse. A reused address is an immediate clustering anchor. Even a single reuse — a darknet market address also used for a personal purchase — can collapse an entire privacy strategy and link multiple wallets to a single individual.

CoinJoin and Collaborative Transactions

CoinJoin represents one of the most effective privacy-enhancing techniques available for Bitcoin. CoinJoin is a trustless mixing protocol where multiple users collaboratively construct a single transaction with inputs from each participant and outputs of equal denominations to each participant. By mixing coins in this manner, CoinJoin breaks the common input ownership heuristic and creates ambiguity about which inputs fund which outputs, significantly degrading transaction analysis effectiveness.

The CoinJoin process works as follows:

  1. Multiple users connect to a coordination service or peer-to-peer network and express intent to participate in a mix.
  2. They agree on a common denomination — for example, 0.1 BTC per output.
  3. Each user provides inputs totaling at least the common denomination plus fees and provides a fresh output address.
  4. The coordinator aggregates all inputs and outputs into a single transaction where each participant receives the agreed denomination at their output address.
  5. Participants sign the transaction only if correctly constructed, ensuring the coordinator cannot steal funds.
  6. Once all signatures are collected, the transaction is broadcast to the Bitcoin network.

From an outside observer's perspective, a CoinJoin transaction with ten participants each mixing 0.1 BTC appears as a transaction with ten inputs and ten outputs of equal 0.1 BTC denominations. The observer can see that funds were mixed but cannot determine which input corresponds to which output, creating plausible deniability for all participants.

Several CoinJoin implementations have been developed:

  • Wasabi Wallet integrated Chaumian CoinJoin with zero-knowledge proofs to prevent coordinators from learning the input-to-output mapping. The zkSNACKs coordinator shut down in 2024 amid regulatory pressure.
  • Samourai Wallet / Whirlpool implemented multiple mixing rounds to increase the anonymity set. In April 2024, Samourai Wallet's founders were arrested and charged with money laundering conspiracy, with the DOJ alleging Whirlpool facilitated over $100 million in laundered proceeds.
  • JoinMarket created a decentralized CoinJoin marketplace where users can take liquidity from market makers who earn fees for providing mixing services, enabling trustless mixing without central coordinators.

The regulatory environment surrounding CoinJoin has become increasingly hostile. U.S. DOJ prosecutors have characterized CoinJoin implementations as money transmission services requiring licenses and subject to AML regulations. OFAC sanctioned Tornado Cash, an Ethereum mixing protocol, for facilitating money laundering; similar actions could target Bitcoin CoinJoin services. Some centralized exchanges block deposits from addresses that have participated in CoinJoin, treating mixed coins as tainted.

INVESTIGATIVE NOTE CoinJoin participation is identifiable on-chain by the equal-denomination output pattern. Blockchain analytics platforms flag addresses associated with CoinJoin activity. Server seizures of CoinJoin coordinators (where applicable) may yield user databases that deanonymize mixing participants. Users who employed Wasabi or Samourai prior to those services shutting down may still have mixed coins in their wallets, creating detectable patterns.

Lightning Network Privacy and Taproot/Schnorr Signatures

Lightning Network Privacy Characteristics

The Lightning Network provides enhanced privacy by conducting transactions off the Bitcoin blockchain. Lightning transactions are not recorded on-chain except for channel opening and closing events. This means that intermediate hops in payment routing, transaction amounts, and payment counterparties are not visible to blockchain observers.

While Lightning has its own privacy considerations — including channel capacity analysis, routing metadata, and the potential for node operators to log payment information — it provides substantially better privacy than on-chain transactions for many use cases. For investigators, a suspect who receives payment via Lightning and then settles to an on-chain wallet creates a gap in the blockchain record. The on-chain evidence shows channel open and close, but intermediate payments are visible only to participating nodes.

Taproot and Schnorr Signatures: Privacy Implications

Bitcoin's November 2021 Taproot upgrade (BIP-340, 341, 342) introduced privacy enhancements without implementing mandatory privacy, enabling Bitcoin's continued regulatory acceptance while improving privacy for users choosing sophisticated transactions.

  • Schnorr Signatures replaced Bitcoin's ECDSA. The key privacy benefit: Schnorr enables signature aggregation — combining multiple signatures into a single compact signature. Previously, multi-signature transactions revealed the number of signers and transaction complexity on-chain. With Schnorr signatures, multi-signature and complex smart contract transactions appear indistinguishable from simple single-signature transactions.
  • Merklized Alternative Script Trees (MAST) enable complex smart contracts to reveal only the executed path rather than all possible execution paths. Only the transaction condition that was met is visible on-chain; alternative conditions and backup logic remain hidden in a Merkle tree.
  • Transaction size reduction: Schnorr signatures and MAST reduce transaction data size, enabling more transactions per block and reducing fees. Smaller, more uniform transactions make transaction types less distinguishable.

By October 2025, approximately 85% of new Bitcoin transactions employed Taproot addressing. For investigators, Taproot means that:

  • Multi-signature transactions are harder to identify on-chain
  • Complex scripts may have hidden conditions not visible in the spending transaction
  • The uniformity of Taproot transactions reduces the effectiveness of some transaction-type heuristics
  • Taproot does not prevent clustering, exchange attribution, or IP-based deanonymization

Investigative Implications of Privacy Techniques

The fundamental investigative principle: privacy techniques on Bitcoin create friction, not impossibility. A suspect who uses CoinJoin may delay your investigation and complicate attribution, but they cannot erase the blockchain record. The funds still moved. The addresses still exist. The exchange deposit still occurred. The IP log was still recorded (if captured). The behavioral pattern still leaked. Your job is to build a case through the friction, using corroboration, alternative techniques, and the reality that perfect operational security is extremely rare.

The transparency that makes Bitcoin attractive to early cypherpunks actually makes it less suitable for illicit finance than traditional cash. Industry analyses consistently estimate that illicit transactions represent less than one percent of overall Bitcoin transaction volume — a far lower percentage than estimates for fiat currency illicit use. This suggests that sophisticated criminals increasingly recognize Bitcoin's investigative exposure and migrate to privacy coins, cash, or traditional financial system vehicles that offer better operational security.

For investigators, this is the ultimate advantage: Bitcoin's blockchain is a permanent record. Every transaction is recorded forever. Every mistake is preserved. Every link to identity, once made, is irreversible. The suspect who believes Bitcoin provides perfect anonymity has already lost.

Investigator Checklist — Privacy Technique Impact Assessment
☐ I have identified whether the suspect used CoinJoin, Whirlpool, Wasabi, or other mixing services
☐ I have assessed whether mixing transactions prevent definitive attribution or merely create evidentiary challenges
☐ I have checked whether any mixing service has been subject to server seizure or law enforcement action
☐ I have evaluated whether Taproot usage affects the heuristics I planned to apply
☐ I have considered whether Lightning Network usage creates off-chain evidence gaps
☐ I have identified whether PayJoin may have contaminated clustering results
☐ I have documented the anonymity set size for any identified CoinJoin transactions
☐ I have evaluated whether exchange KYC records can overcome mixing by linking withdrawal to identity
☐ I have considered temporal analysis and behavioral patterns as alternatives when mixing breaks clustering
☐ I have consulted blockchain analytics platforms for entity tags and mixing service attribution

questions.q: A detective is reviewing a Bitcoin transaction and notices that the inputs total 2.5 BTC while the outputs total 2.498 BTC, with no explicit fee output. Where did the remaining 0.002 BTC go?
options: It was destroyed by the network as an anti-spam measure
It was returned to the sender's original input address automatically
It was collected by the miner who included the transaction in a block
It was held in the mempool pending a second transaction to collect it

options: Legacy P2PKH — the suspect is using Bitcoin's original 2009 address format
P2SH — the address likely represents a multi-signature wallet configuration
Native SegWit (Bech32) — the suspect is using wallet software from 2017 or later
Taproot (P2TR) — the suspect is using post-2021 wallet software; multi-sig transactions may appear indistinguishable from single-sig
